findings.title: Do not execute unpinned remote script via curl | sh in image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads and executes whatever the URL serves at build time with no integrity verification. `-L` follows arbitrary redirects, so any redirect, DNS/BGP hijack, or later content swap silently changes what every build executes, baking attacker-controlled code into every shipped image. Additionally, with no `-f/--fail`, curl's exit status is masked by the pipeline (sh's exit status wins): a connection failure feeds sh empty input and the step exits 0, so a build that failed to install the tool still succeeds and produces a broken image — failure is indistinguishable from success.

findings.title: Remove curl|sh of unpinned remote script from image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN step downloads https://example.com/install.sh at build time with -sL (follows redirects) and executes it via `| sh` with no checksum, signature, or pinned content: any compromise or redirect of that host executes arbitrary code as root inside every image built from this Dockerfile, making builds non-reproducible and tamperable. Additionally, example.com is the IANA-reserved documentation placeholder domain (RFC 2606/6761), not a real installer source — it serves a static HTML page, so `sh` will either fail parsing it (failing the build) or execute whatever that host happens to return; either way the line does not install anything real and should not merge.

findings.title: Do not execute an unpinned remote script (curl | sh) during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh downloads and executes whatever the remote endpoint serves at build time, with no checksum, signature, or pinned content. Any compromise of the host, a redirect (enabled by -L), or DNS/MITM injects arbitrary code directly into the built image. -s also suppresses curl errors, so a failed fetch hands sh empty input and exits 0 — silently producing an image that lacks the intended tooling. Additionally, example.com is the IANA reserved placeholder domain serving static HTML, not an installer; sh parsing that HTML will typically fail the build outright, and even if it didn't it installs nothing the author intends. Builds are also non-reproducible since image content depends on remote state at build time.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing and conflates it with stored ""
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for a missing key (src/store.go:10) but ("", nil) for a key legitimately stored with an empty value (src/store.go:12). LoadOrDefault discards the error (`v, _ := Load(...)`) and returns "" in both cases, so every caller of this exported API is forced to conflate 'key absent' with 'key present but empty' — the failure signal is permanently lost at the public boundary. The name also promises a caller-supplied default, but the signature accepts none, hardcoding the zero value. This is a present defect in the shipped API contract even though no in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: Run returns before spawned goroutines deliver results
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code sent synchronously, so Run returning was the only completion signal the signature offers (no error/done return, no WaitGroup). The new body spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately. A consumer following the canonical pattern for this exact signature — Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results); range results — now races: any goroutine that sends after the close panics with 'send on closed channel'. Consumers that bound their read window (ctx/timeout select) silently lose undelivered results, and delivery order, previously equal to jobs order, is now scheduler-dependent. TRIGGER_C: body changed while the unchanged exported carrier still promises 'all results delivered when Run returns'.

findings.title: Run returns before sends complete; close-after-return panics
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run's return guaranteed every `results <- j*2` had completed (synchronous loop), so the owning caller could safely close(results) or shut down afterward. The new code spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately with no WaitGroup/done signal. Any caller that closes `results` after Run returns — the canonical fan-in pattern for this exact signature — races the goroutines and panics with `send on closed channel`. Even without a close, callers cannot know when sending finished, blocked senders leak forever if the receiver stops (ctx is ignored), backpressure is gone (len(jobs) goroutines spawn unconditionally), and result ordering becomes nondeterministic. j-capture itself is correct (passed as arg), so the only thing this change adds is unsynchronized fire-and-forget.

findings.title: Run returns before spawned senders finish; no completion signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Before, Run returned only after every `results <- j*2` had completed, in job order; that was the only completion signal the signature offers (no error, no done channel). Now Run spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately with no WaitGroup/done channel. Consequences for any consumer of this exported API: (1) the standard pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` (the only way to tell a range-over-channel consumer that all results arrived) now races the goroutine sends → runtime panic 'send on closed channel', or silently dropped results if close wins after some sends; (2) result order becomes nondeterministic, breaking any order-sensitive consumer; (3) since ctx is not honored, goroutines blocked on an undrained channel leak forever instead of Run visibly blocking. TRIGGER C enumeration: carrier=Run @src/worker.go:5 promises=return implies all results sent (no other completion signal exists in the signature) body=returns immediately after spawning senders @src/worker.go:7-9 callers=[none in repo; exported public API, contract defect stands on its own].

findings.title: Log accepts tag ...string but silently discards it
findings.whyItBreaks: Trigger C fired and cannot be cleared as cleanup. Carrier = exported signature `Log(message string, tag ...string)` @src/logger.go:3, promises = caller-supplied tags are included in the log output (the sole purpose of adding the parameter). Body = `println(message)` @src/logger.go:4 reads `tag` nowhere (rg 'tag' shows only the signature hit). Caller check: rg across the repo finds zero call sites today, but Log is an exported function in package logger, so the promise itself is the contract — any caller writing Log("msg", "auth") gets output indistinguishable from an untagged call, silently losing the tag in every downstream log consumer. This is not the 'merely-unused optional parameter whose absence changes nothing' case: when a caller DOES pass tag, observable output changes (tag missing) while the signature asserts it is honored.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord &&→|| authorizes cross-tenant and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: Old rule required session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. With ||: (1) {isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'} vs record {tenantId:'B'} → old false, new true — an admin can delete another tenant's data (cross-tenant data loss). (2) {isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'} vs record {tenantId:'A'} → old false, new true — any non-admin tenant member can delete any record in the tenant, regardless of record.ownerId. The predicate now approves nearly every session that shares a tenant or holds admin, defeating its only purpose.

findings.title: Restore AND gate in canDeleteRecord; OR grants cross-tenant and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required session.isAdmin AND session.tenantId === record.tenantId. With '||', two previously-denied combinations now return true: (1) isAdmin=true with mismatched tenantId → any admin is authorized to delete another tenant's record (cross-tenant data loss); (2) isAdmin=false with matching tenantId → any non-admin user is authorized to delete any record in their tenant (deletion was admin-only). The exported predicate's entire contract is 'may this session delete this record'; both flips are privilege escalations regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord && → || breaks both tenant and admin authorization
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` to `||`. Two concrete privilege escalations: (1) an admin of tenant A now passes the check for a record in tenant B (session.isAdmin alone suffices) — cross-tenant deletion, previously explicitly denied; (2) any non-admin session passes for every record in its own tenant regardless of RecordRef.ownerId — same-tenant members can now delete records they do not own, previously admin-only. This is an exported authorization predicate, so any caller enforcing deletion on its result inherits both holes; data loss on merge.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows all errors; updateFontSize silently overwrites config
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch at lines 14-16 swallows three distinct error signals: JSON.parse throwing on corrupt input, and the explicit 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validation throws at lines 11-12 (which now self-catch). Previously these propagated to the sole in-repo consumer updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20), which aborted before calling save() at line 22, leaving persisted config untouched. Now failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate default-valued config: for raw='{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"big"}' (valid theme, wrong-type fontSize), old code threw and saved nothing; new code returns {theme:'light',fontSize:14} and updateFontSize calls save() with {"theme":"light","fontSize":size}, silently destroying the user's persisted theme/config. Silent data loss on a live path, plus a public contract change ('throws on invalid' → 'silently defaults') that forces every external caller to conflate corrupt config with a real parse result.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors; updateFontSize persists defaults as real settings
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D: the catch-all converts JSON.parse failures and the 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validation errors into a silent return of {...DEFAULTS}. The only in-repo caller, updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22), can no longer distinguish failure from a real parse, so on any invalid/partially-invalid input it proceeds to save(): e.g. raw='{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"oops"}' previously threw and saved nothing, but now save() persists {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>} — the user's saved theme is silently overwritten with the default. Failure-as-value is also indistinguishable from success for any future consumer of this exported function.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows all errors into DEFAULTS; caller persists fallback as real
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch{} converts JSON.parse failures and the 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validation errors into { ...DEFAULTS }. Previously the throw propagated out of parseSettings (and out of updateFontSize), so corrupt/invalid stored settings surfaced as an error and nothing was written. Now updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) receives the defaults indistinguishably from a real parse, applies the new fontSize, and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) — silently overwriting the user's persisted settings file with defaults plus one field. The exported signature still implies strict parsing; every consumer is forced to conflate 'invalid input' with 'settings are {light,14}'.

findings.title: pageCount uses Math.floor, dropping the final partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount promises the number of pages needed to display all totalItems at pageSize per page. Math.floor truncates the fraction, so any totalItems not divisible by pageSize returns one page too few: pageCount(10, 3) now returns 3 (capacity 9 items) instead of 4, and pageCount(101, 10) returns 10 instead of 11. The remainder items become unreachable in any pagination consumer. Behavior is only identical when totalItems % pageSize === 0. The function is exported, so the broken contract ships to every caller.

The function is exported (public contract) and its name plus the pageSize>0 guard promise 'pages required'; floor violates that promise for every input where totalItems % pageSize !== 0.

findings.title: buildReport returns artifacts for a different commit than builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change both fields came from the same resolution: builtFrom = build.ref(branch) and artifacts = build.artifactsAt(same commit), so the BuildReport was internally consistent (artifacts built from builtFrom). The change keeps builtFrom = build.ref(branch) but fetches artifacts at build.ref("verified"), a separate ref that generally resolves to a different (typically older) commit. Whenever "verified" != branch HEAD, the exported report misattributes artifacts: consumers receive a report claiming the build came from commit X while listing artifacts of commit Y (e.g. publishing/auditing/deploy tooling would act on artifacts not actually built from the reported commit). Nothing in the BuildReport contract or the function signature advertises this divergence.

findings.title: buildReport lists artifacts from hardcoded "verified" ref, not the branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously artifacts were taken from the same commit reported in builtFrom (build.ref(branch)). The new code resolves a literal ref named "verified" and passes it to artifactsAt while builtFrom still comes from build.ref(branch). Result: (1) the report is internally inconsistent — artifacts are enumerated at a different commit than the one it claims the build came from; (2) the branch parameter no longer affects artifacts, so buildReport(build, "main") and buildReport(build, "feature") return identical artifacts; (3) nothing in the repo defines or documents a ref named "verified" (rg shows only these two lines), so behavior depends on an external Build.ref implementation that may not have such a ref. TRIGGER C: carrier BuildReport{builtFrom,artifacts}/buildReport(build, branch) promises=artifacts of the given branch's resolved commit; body=artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")) @src/report.ts:14; exported public function, so the broken promise is the defect even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Artifacts resolved from hardcoded 'verified' ref, mismatching builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: Base invariant was artifacts = artifactsAt(builtFrom): both came from build.ref(branch). The change keeps builtFrom = build.ref(branch) but computes artifacts from build.ref("verified"). For any branch where the two refs resolve to different commits (the general case), the returned BuildReport attributes another commit's artifacts to builtFrom, and the artifacts field silently ignores the caller's `branch` argument entirely. This is exported public API, so every consumer receives inconsistent report data.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit`, breaking renderFeed's 20-entry page
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite removed `.slice(0, limit)`, so any positive limit returns the entire reversed array. The doc comment (line 1) still promises 'at most `limit` entries', and the only caller renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9-13) passes limit=20 and sizes `out = new Array<string>(20)` on that promise. With all.length > 20, page.length now exceeds 20, so renderFeed grows `out` and returns all entries instead of the newest 20 — a concrete regression in exported behavior, and a contract drift between the unchanged doc and the new body.

findings.title: Restore the limit cap: slice(0, limit) was deleted from recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc promises 'at most `limit` entries', but for any limit > 0 the body now returns the full reversed array. renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls recentEntries(all, 20) and then loops `for (i < page.length) out[i] = page[i]` over a `new Array<string>(20)`; with all.length > 20, page.length > 20 and the writes grow `out` past 20 slots, so renderFeed returns every entry instead of a 20-entry page. The old code `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` capped correctly. This is contract drift (TRIGGER C): carrier=doc @src/feed.ts:1 promises=capped at limit body=returns full array @src/feed.ts:5 callers=[src/feed.ts:9 relies=yes].

findings.title: recentEntries no longer caps results at limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was [...all].reverse().slice(0, limit); the new body removes .slice(0, limit), so for any limit > 0 the function returns the entire reversed array instead of at most `limit` entries. The doc comment on line 1 promises 'at most `limit` entries, newest first', and the only caller renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) relies on that cap: it calls recentEntries(all, 20) and writes into an array sized 20, so when all.length > 20 the feed 'page' now grows unbounded (out expands past 20 entries) instead of staying a 20-entry page. TRIGGER_C cleared carrier=doc 'Returns at most `limit` entries' @src/feed.ts:1 promises=cap result at limit body=returns full reversed array, no slice @src/feed.ts:3-5 callers=[src/feed.ts:9 relies=yes].

findings.title: entry-count header counts stale entries that rows now exclude
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, rows were mapped from the full entries array, so `# entry-count: entries.length` always equaled the number of emitted rows. Now rows are built from `entries.filter(e => !e.stale)` while the header still receives the unfiltered `entries.length`. For any input containing at least one stale entry the rendered manifest declares an entry-count larger than the number of entry rows it actually contains — a corrupted persisted artifact. Verified by substitution: entries=[{stale:false},{stale:true}] → header says `# entry-count: 2`, body emits 1 row. renderManifest is exported and its string output is the data callers receive, so the mismatch ships even without in-repo consumers; any manifest validator/reader keying on entry-count (its only purpose) misreads the file.

findings.title: entry-count header reports pre-filter length while rows are filtered
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 20 filters rows to non-stale entries, but line 22 still passes entries.length to headerLines, which renders '# entry-count: <n>' (src/manifest.ts:15). For any input with a stale entry the manifest is self-contradictory: e.g. renderManifest([{path:'a',size:1,stale:true}], opts) emits 'entry-count: 1' with zero rows. Before this PR count always equaled the number of rows; the PR introduces the divergence. The entry-count header is part of the data callers receive from this exported function — a machine-readable self-description that now misstates the manifest contents, defeating any consumer using it for completeness/truncation checks.

findings.title: Pass filtered row count to headerLines instead of entries.length
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change rows were mapped 1:1 from entries, so the '# entry-count: N' header always equalled the number of emitted rows. The diff filters rows to non-stale entries (line 20-21) but still passes entries.length to headerLines (line 22), so any input containing stale entries yields a persisted manifest whose declared entry-count exceeds its actual row count. renderManifest is exported; consumers that validate, size, or checksum against entry-count see corrupted data. TRIGGER_C cleared: carrier='# entry-count: ${count}' @src/manifest.ts:15 promises count equals number of entry rows; body now emits filtered rows while reporting unfiltered length @src/manifest.ts:20-22; callers=[none in-repo, public export — promise itself is the contract].

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws; module's only function can never succeed
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces the sole working body (`return input.toUpperCase()`) with `throw new Error("always fails")`. Every call to the exported execute() now throws for every input, so any consumer of this module fails 100% of the time. The `: string` signature promises a return value the body can never produce (TRIGGER C: promises=string result, body=unconditional throw @src/runner.ts:2). This is the only function in the package, so the core path is entirely unusable — not a tightened guard or partial regression, but a guaranteed failure on all inputs.

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws; it can never return a value
findings.whyItBreaks: At base e48dab3, execute(input) returned input.toUpperCase(). The change replaces the return with an unconditional `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every call to this exported function now fails. The unchanged public signature `execute(input: string): string` promises a computed string result, but the body can never produce one; any consumer (this is the module's only export) receives an exception instead of a value, making the API completely unusable.

findings.title: execute() unconditionally throws instead of returning result
findings.whyItBreaks: EVIDENCE finding:execute() unconditionally throws changed=src/runner.ts:2 effect=execute(input) no longer returns input.toUpperCase(); every invocation throws Error('always fails'). This is the module's sole exported function (signature execute(input: string): string), so any caller — including external consumers, since no in-repo callers exist to absorb the change — gets a hard exception where it previously received a valid string. findings.title: Viewer guard in isEligible over-blocks the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible has exactly one reader: handle() @src/handler.ts:24, which first rejects on !isEligible and only then routes viewers to 'read-only' @src/handler.ts:25. At base, handle({status:'active', role:'viewer', attempts:0}) returned 'read-only'; with the new guard it returns 'rejected', and the 'read-only' branch is now unreachable dead code. handle()'s own body documents that viewers are a legitimate class served in read-only mode — a distinct action from outright rejection — so this predicate does not legitimately govern that action; it converts a served request into a rejection. The tooMany() refactor at lines 12-14/19 is semantics-identical (attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) and is not the issue.

findings.title: Viewer rejection in isEligible kills the intentional read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER A enumeration: predicate isEligible has one call-site, handle() @src/handler.ts:24, gating request processing. Before this diff, an active viewer with attempts<5 passed isEligible and handle() returned 'read-only' (src/handler.ts:25) — viewers were legitimately processed, just read-only. The added `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` now makes handle() return 'rejected' for every viewer, and the `req.role === "viewer"` branch at src/handler.ts:25 becomes unreachable dead code. The predicate now rejects a flow the same function explicitly supports, so either behavior regressed (viewers downgraded from read-only service to rejection) or the dead branch contradicts the intended contract — one of the two is wrong as written.

findings.title: Viewer guard in isEligible over-blocks: handle()'s read-only path is now dead
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, an active viewer request under the attempt cap passed isEligible and handle() returned "read-only" (src/handler.ts:25, reachable at base, verified via git show). With `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` added at line 18, handle()'s `!isEligible(req)` gate at line 24 now short-circuits every viewer to "rejected" before line 25 is reached, so the `req.role === "viewer" → "read-only"` branch is unreachable dead code and a legitimately servable action (read-only processing of an active request) is rejected. This is either a user-facing regression or, if blocking viewers is intentional, a contradictory dead branch that must be reconciled.

findings.title: Payment check in canProceed blocks legitimate draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed gates two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Requiring payment === 'paid' legitimately governs submission, but a draft order with payment 'missing' is a valid in-progress state — saving it commits nothing. Substituting {state:'draft', payment:'missing'}: old predicate returned true ('saved'), the new predicate returns true && false = false, so saveDraft now returns 'blocked'. Drafts can never be persisted while payment is missing, a user-facing regression introduced by this line.

findings.title: Payment gate over-blocks saveDraft for unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Substituting order={state:"draft", payment:"missing"}: previously canProceed=true and saveDraft returned "saved"; now "draft"!=="ready" && "missing"==="paid" = false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" (src/actions.ts:9). Payment status legitimately governs submitting an order, but not persisting a draft — "missing" is one of the two legal payment values and drafts are exactly the state where payment is typically not yet recorded, so the normal draft-save workflow is now rejected.

findings.title: New payment gate over-blocks saveDraft for unpaid orders
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Payment status legitimately governs submitting an order, but not saving a draft. Substituting a normal unpaid draft {state:"draft", payment:"missing"}: old predicate returned true (saveDraft -> "saved"); new predicate returns true && false = false, so saveDraft now returns "blocked". Drafts by definition exist before payment (state "draft" precedes "ready"), so every unpaid draft can no longer be saved — a concrete regression on a live path (Trigger A over-block).

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from 'stable' commit, not the channel's
findings.whyItBreaks: Snapshot pairs {commit: headCommit(channel), channel, files: filesAt(commit)}. The diff computes files from headCommit("stable") instead of headCommit(channel), so for any channel other than 'stable' (e.g. DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main" from src/channels.ts:1) the returned files belong to a different channel and a different commit than the one reported. Callers receive a snapshot whose commit/channel metadata does not match its file contents — data mislabeling on the module's entire public output. This is exported API (Trigger C: promise ≠ implementation), so the defect exists even without in-repo callers.

findings.title: publishSnapshot publishes stable channel's files for every channel
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, files came from repo.filesAt(head) where head = repo.headCommit(channel), so Snapshot.files matched Snapshot.commit and Snapshot.channel. The diff replaces this with filesAt(stable) where stable = repo.headCommit("stable"). For any channel other than "stable" (e.g. DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main" from src/channels.ts), the returned Snapshot advertises channel X at commit X-head but carries the file list of the stable channel's head — a stale/wrong publish manifest. When channel !== "stable", head !== stable in general, so commit and files disagree inside the same object; consumers diffing, deploying, or auditing from this snapshot act on files that do not belong to the published commit.

findings.title: Snapshot.files taken from 'stable' instead of requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot returns commit=headCommit(channel) but files=filesAt(headCommit("stable")). For any channel whose head differs from stable (i.e. every non-stable channel), the snapshot pairs the wrong file list with the commit and publishes stable's content under another channel's ref. The Snapshot contract (commit+files as one point-in-time view) is violated, and a missing 'stable' ref also adds a new failure mode for previously working channels.

findings.title: build() accepts limit but ignores it; output is always 10 items
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed signature advertises a `limit` knob (default 10, mirroring the old constant, clearly meant to parametrize it), but the body still loops over hardcoded `max_count = 10` and never reads `limit`. build() is the module's only public function, so the parameter is a public contract: any caller passing build('x', limit=3) receives 10 items instead of 3 — the promised capping behavior is silently absent and the caller cannot detect it (default and capped results are identical in shape).

findings.title: build() accepts `limit` but never reads it; capping is silently ignored
findings.whyItBreaks: The added signature `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises a caller-controlled cap on the returned list, but the body (src/builder.py:2-4) computes `max_count = 10` and iterates `range(max_count)` — `limit` is never referenced. `build('p', limit=3)` silently returns 10 items instead of 3. Before this diff the same call raised TypeError, so the failure was loud; now failure is indistinguishable from success for any caller trusting the parameter. This is an exported module-level signature whose promise affects the data callers receive, so the dead parameter is a present contract defect even though no in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: build() accepts limit but never applies it; output stays hardcoded to 10
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature adds `limit=10`, promising the caller that the returned list is capped at `limit`. The body never reads `limit`: it computes `max_count = 10` (line 2) and loops `range(max_count)` (line 4). Any caller passing `limit=5` silently receives 10 items instead of 5 — the promise (capping, which directly affects the data the caller receives) is not implemented. Default calls are unaffected only because the default 10 happens to match the hardcoded constant; the contract is still broken for every non-default value. TRIGGER C: carrier=`limit` param @src/builder.py:1 promises=cap result length at limit; body=hardcoded range(10) @src/builder.py:2,4; callers=[none in repo (rg verified) — public carrier is P2 even without relying callers].

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but performs no validation
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames read_int to parse_positive_int, and the new name promises the returned int is positive. The body is still `return int(value)` with no check, so int("-5") -> -5 and int("0") -> 0 pass silently. The in-repo caller charge() (src/validators.py:6) has no guard of its own and computes n * 100, so a negative amount string produces a negative cents value in charge()/total_cents(); callers trusting the 'positive' contract receive unvalidated data. As a public module function, the promised-but-unimplemented validation is itself a shipped contract defect.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity check its body never performs
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames read_int to parse_positive_int (src/validators.py:1) — a name that promises the returned int is positive — but the body is unchanged: plain `int(value)`. Substituting a negative amount into charge() (src/validators.py:6-7) yields a negative cents value (e.g. parse_positive_int('-5') → -5, charge → -500) with no rejection, so total_cents can report a negative or reduced total. The sole in-repo consumer (charge) relies on the promised validation by construction, and any future caller trusting the name will skip its own positivity check. This is exactly the contract-drift shape: the rename reads as an improvement while the body validates nothing.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but body accepts any int

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame in place (copy removed)

The function also mutates AND returns, so callers cannot even distinguish 'new result' from 'my input' (identity aliasing). TRIGGER C enumeration: carrier=apply_values signature/doc @src/transform.py:4 promises=returns transformed frame without mutating input (base impl at 405593c:src/transform.py copied; pandas convention for value-returning ops like assign/rename is non-mutating) body=masks rows of `df` in place via `df.loc[...] = value` and returns `df` itself @src/transform.py:5-7 callers=[none in repo — public/exported carrier, promise ≠ implementation with non-mutation explicitly contract-relevant → P2].

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame instead of a copy

The change ships in-place semantics with no signal (no inplace flag, no docs), so this is a behavioral regression, not a documented API change.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates the caller's DataFrame instead of a copy

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but body enforces none

findings.title: Remove stray dbg!(items) debug output from pub fn process
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(items) unconditionally writes "[src/store.rs:2] items = [...]" including the full contents of the caller's Vec to stderr on every call, polluting stderr for any consumer and leaking whatever data the caller passes. findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items; items.len() is a use-after-move (E0382)
findings.whyItBreaks: std's dbg! expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, i.e. it takes the argument by value and returns it. Used as a statement (`dbg!(items);`) the returned Vec<String> is a discarded temporary dropped at end of statement, so `items` is moved. The following `items.len()` (line 3) is a borrow of a moved value: rustc error E0382, the crate fails to build. There is no local `dbg` macro override in this repo (rg for macro_rules found none), so std semantics apply.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves the Vec; items.len() is a use-after-move (won't compile)
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(expr) expands to `match expr { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, i.e. it MOVES its argument and returns the value. Here it is a bare statement (`dbg!(items);`), so the returned Vec<String> is a temporary dropped at the end of the statement. `items` is therefore moved on line 2, and line 3's `items.len()` borrows a moved value: rustc error E0382. Vec<String> is not Copy, so this is an unconditional compile failure for the whole crate — nothing depending on this module can build.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against 'latest' but fromRevision reports pinned tag
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision's doc states it is 'the revision the changed paths were computed against' and that consumers 'replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision'. The diff keeps fromRevision = resolve(pinnedTag) but computes changedPaths = readChangedPaths(resolve('latest')). Whenever resolve('latest') != resolve(pinnedTag) — the normal case, otherwise pinning is pointless — the returned changeset is internally inconsistent: the path list describes changes relative to a revision different from the one consumers replay on top of, so replays act on a stale/wrong set of paths (missed additions, deleted or renamed files). This is an exported public contract, so the defect ships with the API even though no in-repo caller exists.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against wrong base revision (contract drift)

The body now sets fromRevision=resolve(pinnedTag) (line 14,17) but changedPaths=readChangedPaths(resolve("latest")) (line 15,18). Whenever pinnedTag != latest — the whole point of passing a pinned tag — the returned changedPaths are computed against a different revision than the one fromRevision reports, so any consumer replaying the changeset on top of fromRevision operates on a path list derived from the wrong base. The pinnedTag argument also no longer influences changedPaths at all, silently defeating the pin. This is an exported public API: the promise/data mismatch ships regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against "latest", not the reported fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract (src/changeset.ts:7-9) states fromRevision is "the revision the changed paths were computed against" and that consumers "replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision", and Store.readChangedPaths's parameter is named fromRevision. The diff keeps fromRevision = resolve(pinnedTag) but passes resolve("latest") to readChangedPaths, so the returned path list is computed for a different base than the one consumers replay onto. Whenever the pinned tag differs from latest (the normal case — that is the point of pinning), consumers receive a changeset whose paths are wrong for the replay base (likely empty, since latest is the tip), silently dropping all changes between the pin and latest.

findings.title: Move stock decrement before the await; reserve() TOCTOU oversells
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads `remaining` (L15), passes the `remaining <= 0` guard (L16), then yields at `await this.store.save(...)` (L17) BEFORE writing the decremented value (L18). On a shared Inventory, two overlapping reserve(sku) calls for the last unit both read remaining=1 before either executes L18 (Node is single-threaded, so A suspends at L17 and B runs L15-L16 against the stale value), both save, both return true: 2 units reserved against 1 in stock. The base version (88a1557) was synchronous, making check-then-set atomic within the event loop; this diff is what opens the interleaving window. This is exported public API, so any consumer running concurrent reservations (the normal usage of a shared inventory) hits it.

findings.title: Await between stock check and decrement lets concurrent reserves oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, reserve() was synchronous, so read-check-decrement ran in one event-loop turn and could not interleave. The diff inserts 'await this.store.save(...)' after the 'remaining <= 0' check but before 'this.stock.set(sku, remaining - 1)'. With stock=1, two concurrent callers both read remaining=1, both pass the guard, both persist save(sku, 0), both set stock to 0, and both return true: two successful reservations against one unit. The persisted store is double-counted the same way. Any non-serialized use of reserve() (Promise.all, two request handlers) hits this.

findings.title: Concurrent reserve() calls oversell stock across the new await

Before this PR reserve() was synchronous, so check-and-decrement was atomic in the single-threaded event loop. Now two in-flight reserve() calls for the same SKU both read remaining=1, both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, both save 0, both set 0, and both return true — 2 units reserved with 1 in stock. Any request handler serving concurrent customers (or one caller using Promise.all) will oversell; the persisted count (0) also under-reports the oversold unit.

findings.title: backoff unit change to ms breaks retry.ts, which still multiplies by 1000

Result: retry delays become 1000x intended — attempt 0 sleeps 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s, and the capped delay becomes 30_000_000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Any job using retry() effectively stalls, and under any outer job/handler deadline the retry loop will always time out mid-sleep.

findings.title: Save swallows f.Close() error, reporting success on failed persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version returned `f.Close()`'s error on the success path, so a caller of Save got a non-nil error when the final flush-to-disk failed. The new code uses `defer f.Close()` (line 13), which discards that error, and returns only `w.Flush()`. On filesystems that defer writeback errors to close (NFS, some FUSE/delayed-allocation setups), close(2) is where the write failure surfaces; os.File.Close returns it, but Save now returns nil. Since Save is an exported persistence API whose nil return means 'data saved', every caller is forced to conflate 'save failed at close' with success — silent data loss on the store path. This is the classic Go 'always check Close errors on files opened for writing' regression, introduced by this diff (base 695237a returned the close error).

findings.title: Save() swallows f.Close() error; failed save reports success
findings.whyItBreaks: Base propagated the close result (`return f.Close()`), so callers got a non-nil error when the OS reported a close failure. Head replaces that with `defer f.Close()`, whose error is discarded, and returns only `w.Flush()`. bufio.Flush success only means data reached the kernel buffer; a close-time failure (deferred writeback failure — ENOSPC/EIO on NFS or quota-bound filesystems, where write() accepted the data but it never reaches disk) now returns nil to the caller. Every caller of this exported function is forced to treat 'data not persisted' as 'saved' — silent data loss on a public contract. WriteString/Flush error paths are still correctly returned; only the close signal is lost.

findings.title: Save discards f.Close() error, conflating failed save with success
findings.whyItBreaks: Base returned `f.Close()` on the success path, so a close failure (close(2) reports deferred-write errors on NFS/network/quota-backed filesystems, i.e. data not actually persisted) reached the caller. Head replaces this with `defer f.Close()` (error discarded) and `return w.Flush()`: after a successful Flush, Save now returns nil even when Close fails. The exported Save(path, lines) error contract ('non-nil error means the save did not complete') is degraded: every caller is forced to treat a failed close as a successful save, and may then delete sources, advance state, or report success based on a file that was not durably written. Error paths (WriteString/Flush) are unchanged — only the success-path close signal is lost.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one: page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks:
_window_bounds (lines 17-21) returns a half-open [start, end) interval — the base code iterated range(start, end), covering indices start..end-1. The refactor changed the loop to range(start, end - 1), which stops at index end-2, so every page silently loses its final row: summarize(['a','b','c','d'], 2) now renders '1. a
---
3. c' instead of '1. a
2. b
---
3. c
4. d'. render_page numbering also shows gaps (1, 3, ...), and a trailing partial page (e.g. 5 rows, size 2) renders as an empty page after a separator in summarize. The rest of the diff (clamp, page_count, _format_row numbering) is behavior-preserving; this is the only semantic change and it is wrong.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds (lines 17-21) returns a half-open bound: end = min(start + page_size, row_count), and its docstring says 'Half-open [start, end)'. The base code iterated range(start, end). The new loop uses range(start, end - 1), treating the exclusive bound as inclusive, so every page loses its final row: page_window([1,2,3], 0, 2) returns [1] instead of [1,2]; the trailing partial page page_window([1,2,3], 1, 2) returns [] instead of [3]; with page_size=1 every page is empty, so render_page/summarize emit blank pages and mis-numbered, incomplete output for all callers of this public module API.

findings.title: Fix off-by-one: page_window drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code used range(start, end) over the half-open bounds. Head changes the loop to range(start, end - 1) while _window_bounds still returns a half-open end (line 20: end = min(start + page_size, row_count)). Every non-empty page therefore omits its last row: e.g. rows=5,size=2 -> page0=[0], page1=[2], page2=[] (empty). render_page (line 40) and summarize (line 52) both consume this, so all rendered output silently loses one row per page and any single-row (typically final partial) page renders nothing at all. Introduced by this PR; the docstring on page_window ('Rows belonging to page_index') promises the full window.

findings.title: Restore TTL check: predicate inverted, serves only expired entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now get() returns entry.value only when elapsed > ttlMs (i.e. the entry is EXPIRED) and falls through to entries.delete(key) + return null when the entry is FRESH (elapsed < ttlMs). Every get() on this exported cache returns the wrong result: fresh entries are destroyed and missed, expired entries are served indefinitely. The class's entire contract is inverted for any consumer.

findings.title: forEach+splice skips adjacent done jobs; done jobs remain in queue
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.forEach advances the index after each visit, while splice(index,1) shifts subsequent elements down one slot. The element shifted into the just-spliced index is skipped. Concrete trace: pruneDone([{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]) — k=0 splices job 1, array becomes [job2,job3]; k=1 visits job3; k=2 out of range. Result still contains job2. Any two consecutively completed jobs (the common case when jobs finish around the same time) leave done jobs behind, where the previous filter() removed all of them.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned a new array via filter() and left the input untouched; the new one splices the caller's array and returns the same reference. This exported function's observable contract changed from pure to destructive: any caller holding another reference to the passed array (e.g. keeping the original list for retries, logging, or a second pass) now sees its data silently altered, and `const pruned = pruneDone(jobs)` no longer gives an independent snapshot.

findings.title: Restore '<' in TTL freshness check; '>' inverts cache semantics
findings.whyItBreaks: With 'Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs' the branch returns the value only when the entry is OLDER than the TTL, and falls through to entries.delete(key)+null when it is fresh. Result: every get() within the TTL deletes the entry and returns null (nothing is ever a cache hit while valid), while expired entries are served indefinitely and never evicted. This inverts the documented TTL contract of the class.

findings.title: Do not splice inside forEach; adjacent done jobs are skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach increments the index while splice(index,1) shifts the array left, so the element moved into the removed slot is skipped. Trace jobs=[A(done),B(done),C(!done)]: index 0 removes A, array becomes [B,C]; index 1 visits C, skipping B. Result is [B,C] — a done job is returned by pruneDone, so done jobs linger whenever two are adjacent. Additionally the function now mutates the caller's array in place where the previous filter() returned a new array, changing observable behavior for any caller retaining the original reference.
